cues.text: Welcome back.
Newton's laws helped us find acceleration from forces.
Energy gives us another route, especially when a question asks for speed after
travelling a distance.
Start with a ten newton force pulling a block three metres horizontally.
If force and displacement point the same way, the force does thirty joules of
work.
A joule is one newton metre.
Now turn the force through sixty degrees while keeping the displacement
horizontal.
Only the component along the displacement contributes to work.
Ten times cosine sixty degrees is five newtons, and five times three gives
fifteen joules.
That is why the constant force equation is work equals force times displacement
times the cosine of the angle between them.
The angle is not automatically the angle to the ground.
Identify the actual displacement first.
Holding a heavy bag still can feel tiring, but the upward force does zero
mechanical work on the stationary bag because its displacement is zero.
This definition describes energy transfer to the object; it does not measure
how tired a person feels.
Work can be positive, negative, or zero.
The sign tells us how a force contributes to the energy balance.
A pull along the displacement does positive work.
Kinetic friction on a block sliding across a stationary floor acts opposite the
displacement, so it does negative work.
On that same horizontal floor, weight and the normal reaction are perpendicular
to the displacement and do zero work.
They still matter: the normal force may determine the friction.
Zero work does not mean an absent force.
Think about uniform circular motion.
The centripetal force continually changes the direction of velocity, but
remains perpendicular to the instantaneous motion.
It therefore does no work, and speed stays constant.
Here is your check before calculating: name the force, identify the
displacement, and decide the angle.
Do this separately for every force.
Never assume that all contact forces do negative work in every possible
situation; the moving surface and the chosen object matter.
Kinetic energy is one half times mass times speed squared.
It is a scalar, so reversing the direction of motion alone does not change it.
If speed doubles, kinetic energy becomes four times as large.
The work energy theorem says net work done on a particle equals its change in
kinetic energy.
Why does that connect to Newton's law?
For constant net force along a straight line, combine force equals mass times
acceleration with v squared minus u squared equals two a s.
Multiplying force by displacement gives one half m times v squared minus u
squared.
The theorem also holds with changing forces when work is calculated correctly
along the path.
Try an example.
Fifty joules of net work act on a four kilogram particle initially at rest.
What speed results?
Think before substituting.
Fifty equals one half times four times v squared.
Therefore v squared is twenty five, and speed is five metres per second.
Use net work, not just the work of the most visible force.
Zero net work means equal initial and final speeds; it does not guarantee
unchanged direction or zero acceleration throughout the journey.
Let us solve a stopping problem using energy.
A two kilogram block slides at ten metres per second and stops after five
metres on a rough level floor.
Assume friction is the only force doing work.
We want the average magnitude of the friction force over this distance.
Start with the initial kinetic energy: one half times two times ten squared
equals one hundred joules.
The final kinetic energy is zero.
The change is minus one hundred joules.
Friction acts opposite the displacement, so its work is minus F times five.
Equating the two gives F equal to twenty newtons.
The minus sign belongs to the work, while the requested force magnitude is
positive.
Pause and ask what would change if the initial speed doubled while mass and
friction stayed the same.
Initial kinetic energy would be four times larger, so the stopping distance
would also be four times larger.
This is a useful JEE comparison because you can answer it without calculating a
stopping time.
State the constant friction assumption when making that comparison.
Finally, connect work to a falling object.
A half kilogram stone falls ten metres from rest.
Use g equal to ten metres per second squared and neglect air resistance.
Gravity does positive work because force and displacement point downward.
Its work is m g h: one half times ten times ten, or fifty joules.
That becomes kinetic energy.
Fifty equals one half times one half times v squared, so v squared is two
hundred and the speed is approximately fourteen point one metres per second.
The mass cancels from the final speed under these assumptions.
You can also describe this as gravitational potential energy becoming kinetic
energy.
Near Earth's surface, a vertical drop h reduces gravitational potential energy
by m g h.
Mechanical energy stays constant when only conservative forces do work in the model.
If friction or drag removes mechanical energy, include that work; total energy
is not destroyed, but some becomes thermal energy.
Before finishing any energy problem, check the object or system, the forces
doing work, the initial and final states, and the signs.
These foundations prepare you for later lessons on springs, power, and
collisions.
